extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne / educated readers of early modern essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading of Montaigne's Essays (selected chapters) discussing the vanity of grandeur, sumptuary laws, sleep, battle conduct, and names; the excerpt mixes moral/philosophical prescriptions, social observations, and illustrative anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of external goods relative to internal state
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Plato is in the right when he tells us that health, beauty, vigour, and riches, and all the other things called goods, are equally evil to the unjust as good to the just’ — external conveniences serve little use when body and mind are in disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that pleasures and goods are mediated by an individual's internal condition: pain, sickness, or passion can deprive one of any enjoyment these externals might offer; therefore, wealth or rank add little to true happiness unless the person is rightly constituted. Examples: a gouty prince loses relish for luxury; grandeur cannot stop basic human reactions like blushing or anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and cost of ruling vs private life
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is far more easy and pleasant to follow than to lead; and that it is a great settlement and satisfaction of mind to have only one path to walk in, and to have none to answer for but a man’s self.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recommends caution toward ambition: ruling imposes burdens, public scrutiny, and responsibility that often outweigh the supposed pleasures of sovereignty. He cites anonymous authorities (Seleucus, Hiero) and classical sayings to show virtue and contentment are often better preserved in private life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur diminishes authentic friendship and mutual society
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Hiero ... finds himself stripped of all friendship, deprived of all mutual society … The honour we receive from those that fear us is not honour; those respects are due to royalty and not to me.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a ruler's attendants and subjects are constrained by duty and fear, apparent respects are not reliable signs of genuine affection. Montaigne treats authentic social bonds as central to human flourishing and sees sovereignty as isolating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of the great amplifies their faults
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The blemishes of the great naturally appear greater by reason of the eminence and lustre of the place where they are seated, and that a mole or a wart appears greater in them than a wide gash in others.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominence makes small faults conspicuous and subject to harsher judgment; public figures should therefore expect and suffer disproportionate scrutiny. Montaigne uses mythic examples (Jupiter's disguises) to illustrate why the powerful hide or disguise themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satiety of repeated pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Feasts, balls, masquerades and tiltings delight such as but rarely see, and desire to see, them; but having been frequently at such entertainments, the relish of them grows flat and insipid.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overexposure to pleasures turns them tedious to the performer or frequent participant (e.g., choirboys, performers, princes with seraglios). Montaigne uses culinary and entertainment metaphors to show how excess blunts appetite and enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leading by example > prohibitory sumptuary laws
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The true way would be to beget in men a contempt of silks and gold, as vain, frivolous, and useless; whereas we augment to them the honours, and enhance the value of such things … To enact that none but princes shall eat turbot, shall wear velvet or gold lace … is but to bring them into a greater esteem.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes legal restrictions on dress/food (sumptuary laws) as counterproductive: forbidding luxuries increases their desirability. He advises rulers to abandon ostentation themselves; court practice shapes general custom more effectively than statutes. He gives historical examples (Zeleucus, practices of courts) to show alternative social mechanisms for restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal conduct sets popular fashion and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Whatever is done at court passes for a rule through the rest of France. Let the courtiers fall out with these abominable breeches … they will see them all presently vanish and cried down.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne emphasizes the social multiplier effect of court behavior: changes at court rapidly propagate through society without need for laws. Therefore reformers should focus on exemplar behavior among elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism about changing customs and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Plato in his Laws esteems nothing of more pestiferous consequence to his city than to give young men the liberty of introducing any change in their habits … by which means manners are corrupted and the old institutions come to be nauseated and despised.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne, echoing Plato, warns that rapid, fashionable change in harmless customs destabilizes civic life; durable laws are those with long continuance that people accept as ancient. Caution is urged toward novelty in manners, dances, apparel, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sleep as an index of greatness or indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne recounts great men (Alexander, Cato, Augustus, Otho) who slept soundly even before battle or death, suggesting either extraordinary composure or sheer exhaustion; he contrasts instances to question whether sleep is essential or a mark of elevated soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes serve as ethical-psychological evidence: profound sleep in crisis can denote either supreme courage/indifference (Cato, Alexander) or simple physical exhaustion (Marius). Montaigne leaves the physicians to judge whether life depends on sleep, and supplies classical cases to show variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military conduct: aim for the general victory over private concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The aim and design, not of a captain only, but of every private soldier, ought to regard the victory in general, and that no particular occurrences, how nearly soever they may concern his own interest, should divert him from that pursuit.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the Battle of Dreux and examples (Philopoemen, Agesilaus), Montaigne enunciates a practical rule of military ethics: individual impulse or apparent local advantage should not compromise the pursuit of overall victory; commanders must weigh conduct toward general success rather than isolated glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice on naming: prefer easy, well-sounding names
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is really convenient to have a well-sounding name, such as is easy of pronunciation and easy to be remembered, by reason that kings and other great persons do by that means the more easily know and the more hardly forget us; and indeed of our own servants we more frequently call and employ those whose names are most ready upon the tongue.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recommends that parents and historians favor names that are easy to pronounce and memorable. He gives anecdotes (Henry II.) and cites Socrates on parental care in naming; the practical effect is social recall and advantage at court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original names in historical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I am mightily pleased with Jacques Amyot for leaving, throughout a whole French oration, the Latin names entire… I have often wished that such as write histories in Latin would leave our names as they find them and as they are; for in making Vaudemont into Vallemontanus … we know not where we are.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historians and translators: avoid garbling or Latinizing proper names unnecessarily, because altering names detaches persons from place and identity and diminishes clarity and fidelity of historical accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using manor/place-names as surnames
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘Tis a scurvy custom and of very ill consequence that we have in our kingdom of France to call every one by the name of his manor or seigneury; ‘tis the thing in the world that the most prejudices and confounds families and descents.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes the practice by showing how partitions and changes of property scramble genealogies and historical memory; he urges stability in family names to preserve knowledge of descent and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about glory and genealogical pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Let us, in God’s name, satisfy ourselves with what our fathers were contented with, with what we are. We are great enough…’ and elsewhere he observes glory is often only ‘a sound’ or a few dashes with a pen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne counsels modesty and warns that much of noble pretension (fabricated extractions, inflated genealogies, anagrammatic name changes) are vain and unstable; true worth is not secured by names, arms, or records that are easily altered or falsified.
